query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, tuning the Al/Co ratio to control short-range ordering (SRO) stabilizes a partially ordered B2-like network, which governs multi-phase stability and enhances mechanical strength, corrosion/oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composed of a single or dual-phase solid solution, homogenized to minimize pre-existing segregation.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al/Co ratio (e.g., ±5–10 at.% away from equiatomic) to promote or suppress local short-range ordering while keeping Cr, Fe, and Ni near equiatomic.
generation.conditions: Characterize and test these variants under annealing (800–1100 °C) for oxidation resistance, under high-dose ion irradiation for radiation tolerance, and in cryogenic and high-temperature mechanical tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Emergent B2-like short-range-ordered regions centered on Al–Co site clusters within an overall solid solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The local SRO hinders full phase separation, refines dislocation substructures, and promotes stable oxide formation, leading to a combination of elevated temperature strengthening, enhanced environmental resistance, improved radiation damage tolerance, and sufficient ductility at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy variants with moderate Al/Co ratios that promote partial B2-like SRO will show higher yield strength, reduced swelling under radiation, superior oxidation/corrosion behavior, and improved cryogenic toughness, relative to an equiatomic baseline lacking customized Al/Co tuning.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy processed under identical conditions but without systematic adjustment to the Al/Co ratio.
generation.boundary: This enhanced stability is expected only within a limited composition range and temperature window where the SRO phases remain partially stable without forming large-scale intermetallics or excessive segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The sensitivity of such SRO to minor variations (e.g., residual impurities or processing parameters) and the interplay with competing phases requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with discrete steps in Al/Co ratio (e.g., 5 variations), homogenize them, and perform in situ diffraction and microscopy at high temperature and during ion irradiation. Compare phase evolution kinetics, microstructure, and property changes.
measurements: High-temperature in situ X-ray diffraction spectra to detect phase transformations.
Atom probe tomography to measure local compositional fluctuations and short-range order extent.
Mechanical tests at cryogenic and elevated temperatures (yield strength, ductility).
Oxidation and corrosion testing (mass gain, oxide scale analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlling the Al/Co ratio and thus SRO does not affect high-temperature phase stability, oxidation resistance, defect formation under radiation, or cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Are high-entropy alloys the solution to radiation damage? AbstractA body-centered cubic W-based refractory high entropy alloy with outstanding radiation resistance has been developed. The alloy was grown as thin films showing a bimodal grain size distribution in the nanocrystalline and ultrafine regimes and a unique 4-nm lamella-like structure revealed by atom probe tomography (APT). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and x-ray diffraction show certain black spots appearing after thermal annealing at elevated temperatures. TEM and APT analysis correlated the black spots with second-phase particles rich in Cr and V. No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed. Furthermore, nanomechanical testing shows a large hardness of 14 GPa in the as-deposited samples, with near negligible irradiation hardening. Theoretical modeling combining ab initio and Monte Carlo techniques predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich second-phase particles and points at equal mobilities of point defects as the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.

occupying_moves.technique: in-situ X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, atom probe tomography
occupying_moves.conditions: Compositions varied around equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni, tested from cryogenic to elevated temperatures under controlled environmental and radiation exposures

chosen.lever: Al/Co fraction to tune short-range ordering
chosen.technique: High-temperature in-situ diffraction, electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography
chosen.conditions: Systematic Al/Co variations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni, from cryogenic up to service temperatures, including controlled oxidation and/or irradiation
chosen.why: In-situ and advanced characterization techniques provide direct evidence of phase evolution and local ordering as a function of composition and temperature. By measuring structural transitions and correlating them with mechanical, corrosion, and radiation-resistance properties, this experiment directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that short-range ordering and composition control phase stability and the retention of desirable properties in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
